Air Supplement as a Stimulation Approach for the In Situ
Desulfurization and Methanization Enhancement of Anaerobic
Digestion of Chicken Manure
Yunlong Song, Ahmed Mahdy, Zhen Hou, Min Lin, Walter Stinner, Wei Qiao,* and Renjie Dong
Cite This: Energy Fuels 2020, 34, 12606−12615
Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
Article Recommendations
ABSTRACT: Anaerobic digestion of chicken manure produces biogas with an extreme H2S content (5000−6000 ppm), which
greatly weakens the economic viability of biogas plants. In this study, in situ desulfurization through supplying limited air into the
headspace of a digester and the impact upon the process performance were evaluated under diﬀerent oxygen loads (1.4, 2.8, and 4.2
mL/gVSin) and injection approaches (single pulse and continuously). The results showed that an oxygen load at 4.2 mL/gVSin with
continuous injection removed 99.7% of H2S (reduced to 10−15 ppm) and simultaneously increased the methane yield by 6.4%.
Sulﬁde-oxidizing bacteria enrichment and the increased concentration of soluble iron were the main features of the air supplement
system. The 16S rDNA results explained the attached growth of sulfur-oxidizing bacteria on the headspace carriers and the
enrichment of Methanobacterium and Methanoculleus under the microaerated system. The obtained results suggest that in situ
desulfurization technology could be applied more widely.
1. INTRODUCTION
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a promising solution for
stabilizing organic waste, reclaiming bioenergy, and producing
digestate as organic fertilizer. In 2019, China issued a policy
aiming to accelerate the development of bionatural gas,
through the AD of waste, to 20 billion m3 by the end of
2030 (www.nea.gov.cn). In China, around 155 million tons of
chicken manure are produced annually, and regarding its
higher potential biogas production (794 mL/gVS),1 chicken
manure is deemed to be a suitable substrate for AD treatment.
In addition, recent studies indicated that the AD of chicken
manure was successful even under stressed conditions such as
high ammonia level.2,3 However, AD of chicken manure
generates biogas with H2S as high as 5000−6000 ppm, which is
much higher than that produced from the AD of diary manure
(2000−4000 ppm) and sewage sludge (2500−4900 ppm).4,5
Biogas containing high concentrations of H2S could corrode
gas pipes, mechanical devices, and engines, and thus, it must be
puriﬁed before its further utilization.6 A wide range of
desulfurization techniques have been applied, but the
signiﬁcant drawbacks with maintenance complexity, high
cost, and the secondary pollution have restricted their
application.7 So far, a cost-eﬀective approach for removing
H2S from the AD of chicken manure has remained a challenge.
In situ desulfurization technology is proposed as a way of
removing H2S by supplying a limited amount of air/oxygen
into the headspace of an anaerobic digester in which the
growth of sulﬁde oxidizing bacteria (SOB) is sustained. Under
microaerated conditions, SOB biologically oxidizes H2S to
sulfur or sulfate, depending on the O2 dosage (in eqs 1 and 2).8
A wide range of in situ H2S removal eﬃciencies have been
reported for dairy manure (68%; from 4000 to 1120 ppm),4
agricultural waste (88%; from 2500 to 300 ppm),9 and
synthetic waste (99%; from 680 to 10 ppm).10 Recently, H2S
removal from biogas of chicken manure through in situ
desulfurization technology was reported in a batch experi-
ment.11 However, the performance of the in situ H2S removal
in a long-term AD of chicken manure has been scarcely
studied, and the underlying mechanism is still unclear. On the
other hand, improper air dosage may not only result in a lower
H2S removal eﬃciency but also increase the risk of disturbing
the anaerobic environment.12 Balancing the air dosage for
simultaneous H2S removal and an eﬃcient AD performance is
therefore still a challenge. In addition, a stable habitat with
available wetted area is necessary for the bioﬁlm activity,
guaranteeing the eﬃcient H2S removal.13 However, hitherto,
there is little research about the installation of carrier for
bioﬁlm growth during the in situ desulfurization process, and
the microbial features of the bioﬁlm are still lacking and not
quite clear.

phase, and thus the toxic eﬀects of sulﬁde on methanogens
could be alleviated.14 Alongside this, the removal of sulﬁde in
the aqueous phase is assumed to hinder the formation of FeS
and FeS2 precipitation. This leads to the release of soluble iron,
thus improving its potential bioavailability, which has essential
eﬀects on the corresponding enzymes and metabolism of
methanogens.15 So far, though, research into the positive
eﬀects of the air supply on the release of soluble iron in the
anaerobic digesters is lacking.
In addition, it has been reported that air supplement could
signiﬁcantly enhance the diversity and activity of facultative
bacterial communities in the AD system such as some
hydrolytic bacteria, that is, Firmicutes, which could in turn
promote the overall eﬃciency and robustness of the AD
process.16,17 The dominant methanogens group has also been
found to shift when air was supplied.5 It has been reported that
microaeration caused an increase in the Methanoculleus
population,18 while Fu et al. in 201619 found that the genus
Methanoculleus decreased by 43.5% under microaeration
conditions. Theoretically, H2S is generated from the hydrolytic
degradation of proteinaceous materials or the sulfate reduction
process performed by sulfate reducing bacteria (SRB).20 It was
supposed that the in situ removal of H2S may be performed
through two possible pathways: suppressing the sulfate
reduction and/or achieving the H2S oxidation in the digester
headspace.21,22 So far, the discussions about both mechanisms
are limited and controversial; therefore, more knowledge about
the speciﬁc bacteria group involved in above two pathways is
needed. Furthermore, it is worth investigating the hydrolysis,
methane production, and H2S removal process and their
associated microorganisms and mechanisms simultaneously for
further process optimization.
Based on the knowledge obtained from previous batch
experiment, this study, therefore, aimed to evaluate an in situ
biological desulfurization strategy using continuously stirred
tank reactors (CSTR) treating chicken manure under diﬀerent
air dosing conditions. Attention was similarly focused on more
accurately optimizing H2S exclusion and methane production
enhancement simultaneously. The correlation between AD
process parameter indicators was investigated by principal
component analysis (PCA). The microbial community changes
were also investigated through 16S rDNA to further under-
stand the underlying mechanisms of the H2S removal and
improved AD performance.
2. MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1. Substrates and Inoculum. Raw chicken manure with a total
solid (TS) content of 20%−25% was obtained from a chicken farm
located in Beijing. The raw chicken manure was stored in a freezing
room at 4 °C until use. Feathers and sands were removed manually.
The raw chicken manure was diluted, with water, to a slurry with a TS
of around 10%. It was then put into a shredder (Joyoung-JCLC012,
China) before feeding. The volatile solid (VS) and total chemical
oxygen demand (TCOD) of the feeding material were 70 and 101 g/
L, respectively. The inoculum was collected from a lab-scale chicken
manure digester which was operated for more than 2 years under 37
°C.
2.2. Digesters Conﬁguration and Operation Strategy. The
experiment was conducted with two lab-scale CSTRs under
mesophilic conditions, with 10 and 15 L working and total volumes,
respectively. The digesters were equipped with autocontrolled motors
which work at a speed of 150 rpm. The hydraulic retention time
(HRT) was set at 40 days, i.e., daily feeding of 250 mL feedstock. The
organic loading rate (OLR) was ﬁxed at 1.75 gVS (L·d)−1. The system
diagram is depicted in Figure 1.
The two digesters were started and operated in parallel: R1 as
control and R2 as an air supplied digester. Air supplement was applied
to R2 at four stages with diﬀerent injection approaches, namely S0,
S1, S2, and S3. The duration of each stage was 30 days, and the total
experiment lasted for 120 days. R2 was equipped with an air injection
pump with adjustable ﬂow rate (0−500 mL/d). A carrier for bioﬁlm
growth was installed in the R2 headspace near the liquid (5 cm from
the gas−liquid interphase). The carriers were made of nylon rope and
settled with sheet structure by twining around the digester headspace,
occupying one-third of the headspace volume. The diameter of the
carrier was the same as for the digester (20 cm). Before the
experiment started, the carrier was installed in the digester headspace
with spraying sludge on that and injecting a mixture of air and H2S-
rich biogas for SOB group acclimatization and bioﬁlm culturing.
Meanwhile, some additional parts of carrier were dipped in liquid
phase to guarantee the transfer of nutrients and moisture to the
carrier.
The initial air dosage was determined by the H2S content in the
biogas generated from R1 according to the theoretical O2/H2S ratio
(0.5) for H2S oxidation, as shown in eq 1. During the S0 stage (day
1−30), the air was manually injected into R2 at an oxygen load of 1.4
mL/gVS by using the single-pulse (120 mL/d). At the subsequent S1,
S2, and S3 stages, the air was continuously injected at oxygen loads of

Correspondingly, the air ﬂow rates were 5.0, 10.0, and 15.0 mL/h

2.3. Chemical Analysis Methods. The biogas generated was
collected by a gasbag. The biogas volume was measured by a gas ﬂow
meter (LML-1, Jinzhiye Co., LTD, China) and recorded after
calibration under standard conditions. The gas composition was
measured with a gas chromatograph (SP-2100, Beifen-Ruili Analytical
Instrument, China) according to a previous study.23 The H2S
concentrations were measured daily by using a gas detection tube (0−
4000 ppm, Gastec, Japan) and gas composition analyzer (0−1000
ppm, ES-5K, Geotech, UK) from the bag, before the measurement of
the daily gas volume at a high and low levels of H2S, respectively. The
pH was determined by a Mettler-Tolendo pH meter, and the above
parameters were measured daily. The digester eﬄuent was ﬁltered
through a 0.22 μm ﬁlter after centrifugation at 8000 rpm for 20 min
(Cence TGL-16M, China) for volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and soluble
iron analysis. The TS, VS, total chemical oxygen demand (TCOD),
and ammonium (NH4
+-N) were measured according to the American
Public Health Association.24 The compositions of VFAs including
acetate, propionate, isobutyrate, butyrate, isovalerate, valeric acid, and
caproate were measured every 3 days by a gas chromatograph
(Shimadzu GC-2012 plus, Japan). The concentration of soluble iron
in eﬄuent was monitored by an inductivity coupled plasma mass
spectrometer (ICP-MS-X2, Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA) as
described previously.25 Statistics signiﬁcance was obtained by using
one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA, α = 0.05).The H2S
concentration in R1 (control) was regarded as a baseline to calculate
the removal eﬃciency in R2 according to eq 3.

2.4. Statistical Analysis. In this study, the majority of the
analyses were carried in triplicate, and the results were expressed as
mean value ± SD (standard deviation). The correlation relationship
between the AD process parameter indicators was performed by the
PCA method employing the SPSS statistic 25 software package, and
the associated PCA bioplot was drew by Origin Pro 2016 software.
2.5. Microbial Community Analysis. Molecular analysis samples
were collected on day 120, including the samples from the liquid
phase in both digesters and the carrier for the microorganisms in R2;
all samples were collected in duplicate and subsequently stored at −20
°C until tested.2 The method of cetyltrimethylammonium bromide/
sodium dodecyl sulfate was assigned for extraction. Forward primers
(338F and 524F) and reverse primers (806R and 958R) for bacterial
and archaeal sequences, respectively, were performed for ampliﬁca-
tions of 16S rDNA. The key characteristics of PCR thermal cycling
were taken from a previous study.3 PCR products were then puriﬁed,
quantitated, and paired-end-sequenced based on the platform of
Illumina MiSeq Ultimately, to remove the poor-equality sequences,
the Majorbio I-Sanger Cloud software (www.i-sanger.com) was
assigned to analyze the primary data. The sequences were rareﬁed
to 25000 sequences per sample, and those with 97% similarity were
integrated into operational taxonomic units (OTUs). Taxonomic

3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
3.1. H2S Removal Eﬃciency with Diﬀerent Air
Injection Strategies. In the R1 (control), the H2S
concentration in biogas was 5500 ± 400 ppm, which was
comparable to previously reported values in chicken manure
digesters.26 This value was utilized to determine the air
injection dosage in R2. Initially (at S0 stage), air was supplied
by injecting air at 120 mL/d by a single pulse. The H2S
concentration in biogas decreased dramatically to around 1500
ppm, representing a H2S removal eﬃciency of 68%. The lower
H2S removal eﬃciency obtained at the S0 stage may be
attributed to the partial consumption of oxygen by other
facultative microorganisms instead of SOB, resulting in the
insuﬃcient oxygen for subsequent H2S removal.27 It was
anticipated that the removal eﬃciency could be improved
when matching the air injection with the H2S generation rates.
Hence, from the 31th day (at S1 stage), the same daily amount
of air was continuously injected with a ﬂow rate of 0.08 mL/
min (5 mL/h). The H2S removal eﬃciency attained
consequently increased to 86% (Figure 2).
To improve the O2 availability for SOB and then further
enhance the H2S removal, the air ﬂow rate was increased to
10.0 and 15.0 mL/h during the S2 and S3 stages.
Consequently, the H2S removal eﬃciency reached 97% and
99.7% in S2 and S3, respectively. The H2S content in biogas
and methane production was measured every 4 and 2 h after
feeding, respectively, lasting for 20 h. As shown in Figure 3b, it
is obvious that the H2S content in biogas maintained a low
level (<100 ppm) after feeding and sustained to decrease,
ﬁnally, to <20 ppm. It veriﬁed the hypothesis that higher
availability of O2 from increased air dosage for the SOB group
signiﬁcantly improved the eﬃciency and stability of the H2S
removal process. In practice, to maintain the feasibility of
subsequent utilization and reduce the risk of explosion because
of the mixture of methane and oxygen, it is important to note
that resident O2 in biogas is undesirable. Therefore, the
resident O2 in biogas at diﬀerent stages was measured. In Table
2, the O2 content in biogas was almost negligible and was far
from the ﬂammable range of 5−15% of methane.28
3.2. Enhancement of Methane Production with Air
Injection. The cumulative methane production in R1 and R2
is shown in Figure 4a. The average cumulative methane
production of R1 at each stage is 186 L, while that of R2 is 176,
194, 196, and 198 L at the S0, S1, S2, and S3 stage,
respectively. In addition, calculated by characteristics of
feedstock, the mean methane yield of R1 was 345 ± 12 mL/
gVSin, and the methane yield of R2 at the S0 stage was 329 ±
28 mL/gVSin (Table 2). The decreased methane yield was also
reported when the chemically precipitated primary sludge was
treated with a semicontinuous injection at 500 mL of air/d.29
The relatively lower methane yield may be ascribed to the
unbalanced air injection. The methane yields in R2 with
continuous air injections increased to 360 ± 13, 363 ± 18, and
367 ± 14 mL/gVSin during the S1, S2, and S3 stages. They

performance obtained in this study, the ﬁrst-order kinetics
model was assigned to simulate the biogas production in R1
and R2. The methane production rate in R2 at S3 had a higher
K1 (0.098) than that (K2 = 0.088) in the control (Figure 3a).
The raised methane production rate in R2 may be ascribed to
the acceleration of facultative microorganisms with the
existence of oxygen and the relieving of H2S on micro-
organisms.30 In addition, Figure 4c illustrates that the VFAs in
R2 maintain a lower level than that of R1. More speciﬁcally,
the mean VFA concentrations were 494, 485, and 430 mg/L in
R2 during the S1, S2, and S3 stages, which demonstrated a
remarkable 21.1%, 22.6%, and 31.5% reduction compared to
that of R1 (626 mg/L). Also, the acetate and propionate
content in R2 maintained a lower level compared to that in R1
(Figure 4d,e). The acetate in R2 constituted a larger
proportion of the total VFAs at a higher oxygen load (4.2
mL/gVSin) compared to R1 (78.9% vs 68.1%); this was also
consistent with the previous study, which may be ascribed to
the acceleration of degradation and oxidation of unexpected
VFA to acetate under microaeration conditions.31,32 The lower
VFA level and absence of longer fatty acids accumulation, that
is, propionate, were reported to improve the AD process
stability and higher methane yield.33 Table 3 summarizes
studies on H2S removal eﬃciency and methane yield
enhancement.
Considering the ionization equilibrium of H2S, HS−, and
S2−, the removal of H2S from the biogas would therefore
reduce the free S2−concentration in the liquid phase.
Consequently, the Fe2+ which was previously precipitated by
S2−may be “released”. The soluble iron concentration in the
two digesters is shown in Figure 5. With the improvement of
H2S removal eﬃciency, the soluble iron in R2 became
signiﬁcantly higher than that in R1. During the S3 stage, the
soluble iron in R2 increased to 75.8 mg/L, which was higher
by 1.4-fold than that of R1 (54.7 mg/L).The raised soluble
iron content in R2 may be ascribed to the mitigation of sulﬁde
in the liquid phase, which blocks precipitation of FeS and
“releases” free iron, improving the bioavailability of iron for the
microorganism. It was reported that addition of a minute
amount of Fe2+ or Fe3+ has a signiﬁcantly positive eﬀect on the
AD performance of swine and dairy manure.37,38 The raised
soluble iron content attained in this study has a positive eﬀect
on the methane yield, as shown in Figure 5.
3.3. Correlation between System Operation Param-
eters and Air Injection. In Figure 6, the PCA was employed
to assess the potential correlation among the parameters. In
total, air injection dosages and other AD process parameters
were collected at diﬀerent stages (S0−S3) with various air
strategies. Obviously, the two axes in the PCA plot were noted
as PCA1 and PCA2, annotating 65% and 22% of the total
variance of related data, respectively. PCA plot indicates that
the 12 samples were clustered in three areas: (1) T1, T2, T3
(S0), (2) T4−T11 (S1−S3), and (3) T12 (S3). This suggests
that the air injection strategy before entering the optimized
stage signiﬁcantly aﬀected the H2S content in biogas and VFAs
level since the two parameters were clustered in the top-left
quadrant in the PCA bioplot. However, after shifting to
continuous air injection, higher air injection dosages (T7−T12
at S2 and S3) have signiﬁcantly positive eﬀects on methane
yield, soluble iron concentration, and methane content,
whereas pH, VFAs, and H2S were discrepant from the
direction of raised air dosages. The presentation of PCA plot
was in tangent with the same tendency in Figures 2 and 4. The
raised air dosage could improve the AD performance and
stability, which may be ascribed to the remission of inhibition
of sulﬁde on the microbial community and enhancement of
hydrolytic bacteria under microaeration conditions, degrading
more complex substrates to VFA and subsequently converting
more VFAs to methane. The results obtained evidenced that
the most signiﬁcant factor is air injection dosage, which
directly determines the H2S removal eﬃciency and lower level
of VFAs, consequently reﬂecting on enhancement of methane
yield. Furthermore, the PCA results illustrate that continuous
air injection with slightly excessive air density was more
beneﬁcial for AD performance.
3.4. Sulfate Reducing Bacterial Population Structure.
The SRB population in the R1 and R2 during the S3 stage was
evaluated. The 16S rRNA gene sequencing results indicated
that several genera of SRB were identiﬁed in both R1 and R2 at
relatively low levels. The relative abundance and metabolism
characteristics of this SRB group are listed in Table 4.

hydrogen, lactate, and ethanol as an electron donor.39 With the

3.5. Bacterial Community in the SOB Carrier and
Liquid Phase. The SOB team is commonly known to be the
main contributors to biological H2S oxidation. For instance,
Jenicek et al. in 201141 demonstrated that SOB group activity
was greatly enhanced with the existence of O2, and it helped
attain 99% removal of H2S. To identify the SOB group
responsible for H2S oxidation in this study, the biosamples
were gained from the liquid phase and bioﬁlm of the carrier at
the 120th day (S3). As shown in Figure 7, on the carrier, the
phylum Firmicutes dominated among the members with a level
of 64% while phylum Proteobacteria and Actinobacteria were
observed to occupy 2.8% and 1.2%, respectively. It was
observed that the majority of SOB members belonged to
phylum Proteobacteria and Actinobacteria with genera
Halothiobacillus and Sulfuricurvum as the most frequently
cited genera.42 The SOB populations on the carrier were
detected to be at a relatively low abundance among the
bacteria community (2.7%). This was dominated by genus
Fastidiosipila (24%), followed by Proteiniphilum (15%) and
Caldicoprobacter (6%). In Table 5, genus Sulfuricurvum,
belonging to ε-Proteobacteria, was identiﬁed with a higher
relative abundance (0.96%) compared to other SOB genera,
and it was dominant among the SOB members, followed by
Thiobacillus (0.78%), Acinetobactor, belonging to γ-Proteobac-
teria (0.76%), and Pseudomonas (0.23%). Sulfuricurvum sp.,
classiﬁed as an autotrophic genus, was reported to grow
facultatively, and this genus was capable of oxidizing sulﬁde,
elemental sulfur, and thiosulfate while also causing the
accumulation of elemental sulfur extracellularly.43As for the
genus Thiobacillus, some members belonging to which was a
chemolithotrophic SOB group, it has been commonly studied
and reported to be the most appropriate microbes for sulﬁde
removal due to its rate of sulﬁde oxidation, modest nutrition
requirements, and higher aﬃnity for sulﬁde and oxygen.44 This
SOB group could oxidize a variety of sulfur compounds. The
genus Thiobacillus sp. and Pseudomonas sp. identiﬁed in this
study could be responsible for the oxidation of the
intermediate products of some reduced organic sulfur
compounds such as H2S.45 In addition, these genera of SOB
were also identiﬁed in the liquid phase of both digesters; the
SOB population identiﬁed in R2 liquid phase may also
contribute to the eﬃcient sulﬁde removal in the liquid phase.

control, it could be explained that some species of SOB such as
Thiobacillus thioparus could grow under anaerobic conditions,

The bacterial community in the liquid phase of R1 and R2 is
shown in Figures 7 and 8. The diversity of the bacterial
community in R2 was higher than R1, displaying a higher
Shannon index (4.2 vs 3.9) and a lower Simpson index (0.04 vs
0.06) compared with the control group. The higher diversity in
the microaerated digester has also been described by Lim et al.
in 2014.16 Figure 7 illustrates that phylum Firmicutes
dominated R1 (57%) and R2 (64%) followed by the
Bacteroidetes (22% and 25%) and Cloacimonetes (11% and
5%). Firmicutes is capable of producing several extracellular
enzymes, that is, carbohydrase, protease, and lipases, which
degrade diﬀerent kinds of organic matter. The enrichment of
Firmicutes population indicated the acceleration of hydrolysis
and explained higher conversion rate obtained in section 3.2,
supporting the hypothesis of the air supplied digester being a
more favorable habitat for hydrolytic and acidogenic bacteria
and thus accelerating the metabolism of more complex
substrates. Accordingly, in Figure 8a, the relative abundance
of facultative bacteria, genera Fastidiosipila, able to convert
carbohydrate and protein to acetate, was observed to increase
remarkably in R2 compared to that in R1. Also, Gelria, a
hydrogen-producing bacteria, was found to be higher in R2
(3.9%) compared to R1 (2.0%). The relative abundance of
genera Syntrophmonas increased in R2 (4.8%) compared to R1
(3.2%), which is capable of oxidizing acetate and thus able to
work in a syntrophic association with the hydrogenotrophic
methanogens.47 The results of the bacterial community
indicated that limited air injection may facilitate the enrich-
ment of facultatively hydrolytic and syntrophic bacteria, which
could make the hydrolysis in the overall fermentation process
more eﬃcient.
3.6. Methanogenic Community Structure Changes
with Air Injection. The archaeal diversity in R2 was found to
be obviously lower than that of the control digester (R1).
More speciﬁcally, R2 exhibited a lower Shannon index (1.05)
and a higher Simpson index (5.0) compared to that attained in
R1 (1.35 and 3.0, respectively). Air injection was found to
aﬀect the archaeal community structure.17
In Figure 8b, the hydrogenotrophic methanogens Meth-
anobacterium are shown to dominate the archaeal community
of R2, accounting for 75% of all reads followed by
Methanoculleus (14%) and Methanocorpusculum (6%). The
relative abundances of these three archaea were 57%, 8%, and
17% in the R1 without air supplement. The raised percentage
of Methanoculleus in R2 was in accordance with Tang et al. in
2004,18 who reported a signiﬁcant increment of the
Methanoculleus group under microaeration conditions. In
addition, Methanosarcina spp which were acetate and hydrogen
mix-trophic methanogen,48 approximately doubled to 1.6% in
R2. The increased relative abundances of hydrogenotrophic
methanogens may be attributed to following two reasons. First,
the enrichment of syntrophic bacteria (Syntrophomonas) as
discussed in section 3.5 accelerated the synergetic interaction
between hydrogen-producing bacteria and hydrogenotrophic
methanogens. Second, the lower abundance of H2-utilized
SRB, their potential competitors, such as Desulfurovibrio and
Desulfobulbus, provided a more suitable habitat for metha-
nogens to function. The enhanced hydrogenotrophic methano-
genesis with air injection could help maintain lower hydrogen
partial pressure and promote the AD stability.
4. CONCLUSION
Limited air supplement achieved high H2S removal eﬃciency
(>99%) while also enhancing the methane production from
chicken manure AD. Air injections led to lower levels of VFAs
and higher soluble iron content, which explained the improved
AD process performance. The functions of the H2-utilizing
SRB group were restrained, whereas functional SOB members
were strengthened in the air supplied digester. Meanwhile,
higher bacterial diversity, an increment in Firmicutes members,
and hydrogentrophic methanogens, Methanobacterium and
Methanoculleus, explained the improved stability of the process
performance. This study indicated that in situ desulfurization
technology is a feasible candidate for eﬃcient H2S removal in a
conventional biogas plant.
